ABSTRACT

Agriculture plays a significant role in Vietnam’s economic development; however, its distribution chain has many challenges in selling fresh products via e-commerce, including product data management, expiry-based inventory control, multi-warehouse fulfillment, customer care during purchase, and others.

This paper reports the findings of a study “Building an Agricultural E-Commerce System Integrated with ERP and AI Chatbot for Automatic Ordering” that was conducted using Design Science Research methodology. The research introduces the Solaris system, which was prototyped as a Direct-to-Consumer e-commerce marketplace integrated with ERP for product, warehouse, inventory, and order management, as well as a conversational AI chatbot for answering questions and helping with ordering.

The evaluation included functional tests, concurrency checks, and end-to-end checkout benchmarking. The results show that the system can manage dynamic product attributes and multiple selling units, allocate inventory based on expiration dates, and maintain inventory consistency under concurrent checkout. In the 500-user concurrency test, no overselling was detected. The warehouse selection process also considered product availability and delivery distance when assigning complete orders. For AI-assisted checkout, user interactions were reduced by 62.5%, HTTP requests by 57.1%, and average checkout time from 4.48 to 3.63 seconds compared with the conventional checkout process.
Thus, the findings contribute to the body of knowledge by providing a working example of a system that integrates multiple aspects of selling agricultural products via e-commerce with AI assistance.
INTRODUCTION
Research Background

Vietnam’s agriculture sector plays a significant role in the national economy and is directly involved in the country’s food security. In 2025, the agriculture, forestry, and fishery sector contributed around 11.64% to Vietnam’s gross domestic product (GDP). Moreover, the Vietnamese agricultural producers are increasingly interested in not only quantity but also quality, product brands, and standards such as VietGAP and GlobalGAP.

On the other hand, a rapid rise of digitalization, online shopping, and cashless payment has created a new avenue for agricultural producers to sell their products through e-commerce platforms. In other words, the emergence of D2C (Direct-to-Consumer) platforms enables farms and agricultural cooperatives to sell their products directly to the final customer without going through traditional distribution channels. However, agricultural products, especially fresh products, are different from the traditional D2C products in many ways. For instance, agricultural products have a limited shelf life; they may come from different batches and require specific storage conditions during the supply chain, among others. Therefore, agricultural producers need to ensure a systematic flow of goods to meet consumer demands. In other words, a lack of effective management of product information, inventory, and orders fulfills challenges, including problems with inventory management, product expiry, and fulfillment of deliveries of perishable products.
Problem Statement
While online sales channels for agricultural products are expanding, selling and managing fresh produce through e-commerce presents several operational challenges.

Product Data Variability and Multiple Selling Units: Agricultural products may require a wide range of product attributes, including biological characteristics, certifications, and harvest information. These attributes can vary across product categories and may change as product requirements evolve. The same product may also be sold in different packaging specifications and units of measure, such as kilograms, boxes, or crates. Treating these formats as separate items can make product and inventory management more difficult and may result in inaccurate stock availability.

Perishable Inventory Management and Concurrent Checkout: Fresh agricultural products have limited shelf life, and different inventory batches may have different expiration dates. FIFO does not necessarily select the batch with the earliest expiration date. At the same time, concurrent checkout requests may occur when multiple customers attempt to purchase the same limited inventory, creating a risk of inconsistent stock quantities and overselling.

Fulfillment Constraints and Order Splitting: Fresh products are sensitive to transportation time and environmental conditions, making delivery distance an important consideration in fulfillment. In a multi-warehouse environment, items in the same customer order may be assigned to different warehouses. This can result in split deliveries, additional handling, and potentially higher shipping costs.

Conversational AI and Order Completion: Conversational AI can provide a natural-language interface for product search, recommendation, and customer assistance. Existing studies have examined conversational product recommendation and pre-sales dialogue in e-commerce. However, moving from product consultation to actual order completion within the same conversation introduces additional system requirements. In addition, generative AI may provide inaccurate product or inventory information when responses are not based on current system data.

Based on these challenges, this study develops and evaluates Solaris, an agricultural e-commerce platform that integrates back-office enterprise resource planning (ERP) functions with an online storefront and an AI-assisted ordering interface. The study focuses on four areas: flexible product data management, expiry-aware inventory processing, distance-constrained fulfillment, and database-grounded conversational ordering.
Research Objectives

The general objective of the research is to develop and evaluate the Solaris agricultural e-commerce system. The said system is expected to integrate online sales, product and inventory management, fresh-food delivery, and an AI assistant for ordering. The project’s main aim is to improve the management of fresh agricultural products and provide a more convenient experience for the customers.
The specific objectives of the research are as follows: In order to meet the general objective, the research will address four specific technical objectives:

Objective 1 (Dynamic Product Modeling): Develop a dynamic product modeling solution that employs an Entity-Attribute-Value database model combined with a multiple-unit management mechanism to capture product attributes, sellable units, and price tiers in a relational database.

Objective 2 (Expiry-Aware Inventory Control): Design an expiry-aware inventory mechanism that implements First-Expired, First-Out batch allocation with transactional inventory reservations and assess its performance with a concurrency workload of up to 500 users.

Objective 3 (Fulfillment and Warehouse Selection): Implement a distance-constrained warehouse selection mechanism that utilizes distance band batching to allocate entire orders to a single fulfillment hub to minimize order splitting for fresh products.

Objective 4 (Conversational AI and Order Completion): Design a database-grounded conversational AI shopping assistant that enables dynamic product information retrieval and supports order completion through tool calling in chat.
Research Object and Scope
Research Object

This study focuses on the Solaris agricultural e-commerce system and the software features used to manage fresh agricultural products. The main areas covered by the study are product data management, expiry-based inventory management, warehouse selection and fulfillment, and AI-assisted ordering.
The system is designed for an agricultural supply chain that connects farms and cooperatives with consumers in urban areas of Vietnam.
Business Scope
Product and Catalog Management: Product categorization, dynamic product attributes, multiple selling units, and tiered pricing.
Supplier and Purchasing Management: Supplier and cooperative information, purchase order processing, goods receipt, and initial inspection records.
Warehouse and Inventory Management: Inventory batch tracking, expiry dates, stock availability, FEFO (First-Expired, First-Out) picking, and temporary inventory reservation during checkout.
Online Retail and Order Management: Product search, shopping cart management, customer address management, and order checkout.
Fresh-Product Fulfillment: Delivery-distance constraints and assignment of a complete order to a suitable fulfillment warehouse.
Conversational AI Assistant: Natural-language product inquiries, inventory availability checks, and order card generation within the chat interface.
Technology Scope
Backend: .NET 8.0 and ASP.NET Core Web API.
Database: Microsoft SQL Server 2022 Developer Edition.
Frontend: Next.js 14 with Server-Side Rendering for the B2C storefront, and React 18 as a Single-Page Application for the ERP portal.
Artificial Intelligence: Google Gemini API with Function Calling (Tool Calling)[22].
Testing and Supporting Tools: Apache JMeter 5.6.3 for concurrency testing[23], Playwright Core v1.48 for end-to-end testing[24], and VNPAY Sandbox for payment API testing[25].
Research Methodology

This study adopts the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) proposed by Peffers et al. (2007)[1]. DSRM is appropriate for this study because it involves developing and evaluating a software artifact to address practical problems in agricultural e-commerce. The research follows six activities of the DSRM process:

Problem Identification and Motivation: Identify the main operational challenges in fresh agricultural e-commerce, including product attribute variability, perishable inventory, concurrent checkout, order splitting, and limitations in conversational ordering.

Definition of Objectives for a Solution: Translate the identified problems into system requirements and evaluation criteria. These include flexible product data management, concurrent inventory consistency, warehouse-distance constraints, AI grounding, and checkout efficiency.

Design and Development: Design and implement the Solaris system based on the identified requirements. This includes the product data model, inventory management mechanisms, warehouse selection, and conversational AI functions.

Demonstration: Demonstrate the implemented system through representative agricultural e-commerce scenarios, covering workflows from product and inventory management to online ordering and delivery assignment.

Evaluation: Evaluate the system using quantitative tests based on the defined criteria. The evaluation covers schema modification impact, inventory consistency under concurrent checkout, warehouse selection behavior, conversational AI
Communication: Present the system design, implementation, evaluation results, and research findings in this thesis.

Scientific Meaning and Practical Value of the Study.
Scientific Significance

From an engineering perspective, this study demonstrates the integration of established methods, including EAV-based data modeling, FEFO inventory management, spatial distance constraints, transactional inventory control, and tool-enabled conversational AI, within an agricultural e-commerce system.

The study also provides empirical evaluation of these mechanisms in the Solaris system. In particular, it examines the use of a flexible product data model for changing agricultural attributes, expiry-aware inventory allocation combined with transactional reservation during concurrent checkout, distance-constrained warehouse selection, and the use of conversational AI with backend functions for product and inventory information retrieval and in-chat order completion.
Practical Value

From a practical perspective, this study provides a prototype implementation that can be used to demonstrate the feasibility of integrating e-commerce and operational management functions for fresh agricultural products:
For Agricultural Cooperatives and SMEs: The system provides a software foundation that connects online sales with product, purchasing, warehouse, and inventory management within a single platform.

For Fresh Food Retailers: The system provides FEFO-based inventory allocation and temporary inventory reservation to support expiry-aware stock management and reduce the risk of overselling during concurrent order processing.

For Consumers: The system provides delivery-distance constraints for fresh products and an AI-assisted ordering interface that allows customers to check product and inventory information and place orders through conversation.

LITERATURE REVIEW
Overview of Related Studies and Research Gaps
Product Data and Multiple Selling Units
Fresh agricultural products can have many different attributes and may be sold in different units or package sizes. This makes product data more difficult to manage in an e-commerce system.

Niemir and Mrugalska (2021)[2] examined basic product data in e-commerce and found problems with the representation and standardization of product attributes. They also discussed difficulties in exchanging and managing product information across platforms.

Arici et al. (2021)[3] studied the Price Per Unit (PPU) problem. Their work focused on identifying product quantities and units of measurement from product listings so that PPU could be calculated correctly. The required information may appear in the title, description, attributes, or images.

Together, these studies point to two related requirements: product attributes need to be flexible, and quantity and unit information needs to be clearly represented. However, the reviewed studies do not specifically address these requirements together for fresh agricultural products, particularly when products are sold in different units with different prices.
Research Gap (GAP-01): A product data model is needed to support dynamic attributes and multiple selling units with associated prices in an agricultural e-commerce system.
To address this gap, this study uses the Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) model for dynamic product attributes and a multi-Unit-of-Measurement (UoM) mechanism for different selling units and prices.
Perishable Inventory and Online Inventory Commitment

Fresh agricultural products have limited shelf life, and different batches of the same product may have different expiration dates. Inventory management therefore needs to consider both expiry dates and when stock is assigned to customer orders.	Hertog et al. (2014)[4] studied shelf-life modelling for First-Expired, First-Out (FEFO) warehouse management of perishable products. Their work used remaining shelf life to guide inventory rotation and cold-chain decisions.

Figueira et al. (2023)[5] studied inventory commitment in online retail. They proposed allocation policies that commit inventory to customer orders when the orders arrive, rather than waiting until the scheduled delivery time. The policies were also evaluated using real data from a large food retailer.

These studies cover two related aspects of fresh-product e-commerce. Hertog et al. focus on which stock should be used first, based on shelf life, while Figueira et al. focus on when inventory should be committed to an online order. However, the reviewed studies do not specifically examine expiry-aware inventory commitment at the transaction level when several customers are checking out at the same time.
Research Gap (GAP-02): The reviewed studies leave a gap in managing online orders with inventory that is differentiated by batch and expiration date under concurrent checkout.

In this study, FEFO is used to prioritize batches with earlier expiration dates, while inventory reservation is used to hold the required quantity during checkout. The mechanism is evaluated under concurrent order processing to assess inventory consistency and the risk of overselling.
Fresh-Product Fulfillment and Warehouse Selection

Fresh agricultural products may be stored in different warehouses. When a customer buys several products, these products may not be available at the same location. The order can then be split into several shipments.

Zhang et al. (2021)[6] studied split-order fulfillment in multi-warehouse online retailing. Their work focused on package consolidation and considered decisions such as the choice of consolidation warehouse and transshipment. The model aims to reduce the number of packages, shipping cost, and delivery time.

Zhan and Jiang (2022)[7] studied order allocation and last-mile distribution for fresh agriproduct retail. Their model considers order splitting, package consolidation, picking, vehicle scheduling, and multi-temperature delivery. They used an optimization approach to determine order allocation and delivery routes.

Both studies treat multi-warehouse fulfillment as a larger logistics problem with several decisions. This is useful for complex distribution networks, but it is different from the simpler problem considered in this study: selecting one warehouse that can fulfill the whole order and is close enough to the customer.

Research Gap (GAP-03): The reviewed studies do not specifically focus on a simple warehouse-selection rule based on two conditions: sufficient stock for the complete order and acceptable delivery distance.

In this study, a rule-based warehouse-selection mechanism is used. A warehouse is selected when it has enough stock for the complete order and is within a predefined 15 km delivery range. When such a warehouse is available, the order is assigned to that warehouse instead of being split.
Conversational AI and E-Commerce Order Completion

Conversational AI is being used in e-commerce for product recommendation and customer interaction. For an agricultural e-commerce system, it can also be used to provide product information and assist customers during the ordering process.

Rhee and Choi (2020)[8] studied product recommendation through a conversational voice agent in a voice-shopping context. They examined the effects of personalized recommendations and the social role of the agent on customer attitudes toward recommended products. Their experiment showed that both factors affected product attitudes.

Liu et al. (2023)[9] combined a conversational recommender system with a large language model for e-commerce pre-sales dialogue. Their work focused on understanding customer needs and providing product recommendations through conversation. The authors also noted that LLMs may lack the domain-specific knowledge needed for accurate recommendations.

Jiang et al. (2024)[10] studied hallucinations in LLM-enriched product listings. They examined cases where generated information was not faithful to the original product data, showing a reliability issue when LLMs are used to generate product information.

These studies cover product recommendation, pre-sales dialogue, and the reliability of LLM-generated product information. The reviewed work does not specifically focus on a conversational interface that can access current product and inventory data and also complete an order within the same conversation.
Research Gap (GAP-04): The reviewed studies do not specifically address the use of conversational AI for both current e-commerce information and actual order processing in the same conversation.

In this study, the AI assistant uses Function Calling (Tool Calling) to retrieve product, price, and inventory information from backend services and to call order-related functions. An interactive order card is also used to support order completion within the chat interface.
Research Questions
Based on the four research gaps (GAP-01 to GAP-04), this study develops four research questions:

Research Question (RQ1): How can a relational database using the EAV model be designed to support dynamic product attributes, multiple selling units, and multiple price levels for fresh agricultural products?

Research Question (RQ2): How can FEFO and an inventory reservation mechanism be implemented to manage fresh agricultural products according to expiry dates and reduce the risk of overselling when multiple orders are processed concurrently?

Research Question (RQ3): How can warehouse selection and delivery-distance constraints be integrated into a multi-warehouse order process to consider product availability and customer distance while reducing unnecessary order splitting for fresh agricultural products?
Research Question (RQ4): How can Generative AI be integrated with product, inventory, and ordering functions to support customers during shopping and enable order completion within the conversation?

Theoretical and Technical Foundation
Clean Architecture and SOLID Principles

Clean Architecture, introduced by Martin (2017)[11], is applied in the project to isolate the core business logic of the system. This concept adheres to the dependency rule, according to which the dependence between the system’s layers should be directed from the outside inwards. Martin (2017)[11] also offers a list of practices, referred to as SOLID principles, which highlight the basic rules of object-oriented programming.

Specifically, the dependency inversion principle (DIP) is used in the application to invert the dependencies between high-level and low-level modules. According to DIP, a high-level module should not depend on low-level modules; instead, both should depend on abstraction (Martin, 2000)[12]. The application uses DIP to separate business logic from the implementation details of external systems, such as the database, payment system, API, and AI services. Thus, the app’s logic layer depends on the interfaces for these systems, not their particular realizations.
Dynamic Product Data Management and EAV Model

Agricultural products can have different attributes depending on the product type, such as origin, quality, cultivation method, and certification. Some attributes may also change as product requirements evolve. A product database therefore needs to handle attributes that are not the same for every product.

The Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) model is one way to represent this type of data. Dinu and Nadkarni (2007)[13] discussed EAV as an alternative to conventional relational modeling when entities have a large and variable set of attributes. Their study also pointed out implementation issues and limitations, so EAV is more suitable for selected parts of a system rather than as a replacement for the whole relational schema.

In Solaris, EAV is used for product attributes that vary between product categories. Core product fields remain in regular relational columns, while variable attributes are stored using the EAV structure. This allows new product attributes to be added without modifying the main product table.
FEFO Principle and Inventory Management for Fresh Agricultural Products

Fresh agricultural products have limited shelf life, and different batches of the same product may have different expiration dates. Inventory management therefore needs to consider the expiry date of each batch, not only the total stock quantity.

First-Expired, First-Out (FEFO) is an inventory rotation policy in which the batch with the earliest expiration date is used first. Hertog et al. (2014)[4] studied shelf-life modelling for FEFO warehouse management of perishable products. Their work used remaining shelf life as a factor in warehouse and cold-chain management decisions.

Tromp et al. (2012)[14] studied dynamic expiry dates in fresh-food retail. Their work examined how changes in expiry dates can affect product loss, discount decisions, and out-of-stock situations. This supports the importance of expiry information in managing fresh-food inventory.
In Solaris, FEFO is applied at the inventory-batch level. When stock is needed for an order, batches are considered by expiration date and the earlier-expiring batches are selected first.
Geographic Distance and Cold-Chain Considerations

Fresh agricultural products are sensitive to time and temperature during storage and transportation. Mercier et al. (2017)[15] reviewed time–temperature management in the food cold chain and discussed its role in maintaining product quality and reducing food waste.

When the latitude and longitude of two locations are known, the Haversine formula can be used to estimate the great-circle distance between them. It is commonly used for geographic distance calculations based on spherical coordinates.

In a multi-warehouse e-commerce system, this distance can be used as a constraint when selecting a warehouse for an order. However, Haversine gives geographic distance rather than actual road distance. In Solaris, it is used to check whether a warehouse is within the predefined delivery range before the order is assigned.
Multi-UoM Pricing and Order Calculation

E-commerce products can be sold using different units of measurement, such as weight, volume, and count. This is common for agricultural products, where the same product may be offered in different package sizes or selling units.

Arici et al. (2021)[3] studied the Price Per Unit (PPU) problem in e-commerce. Their work showed that product quantity and unit information are important for calculating and comparing prices. The study focused on identifying quantities and their corresponding units from product listings.

For a system that supports multiple selling units, the units need to be represented explicitly so that prices and quantities can be calculated consistently. A conversion factor can be used to relate each selling unit to a common inventory unit.

In Solaris, each selling unit is stored with its conversion factor and price. When an order is placed, the selected quantity is converted to the common inventory unit before stock is deducted and the order total is calculated.
Concurrency Control and Transaction Integrity

Products in e-commerce can be sold in various units of measurement, for example, kilograms, boxes, or pieces. This is particularly relevant in relation to agricultural products, as they involve the use of multiple package sizes.

In this regard, Arici et al. (2021)[3] address the Price Per Unit (PPU) problem in e-commerce through a study aiming at finding a solution to extract quantity and unit of measurement from product listings, which are required to calculate the PPU. Thus, the research highlights the significance of specifying quantity and unit of measurement when providing product prices.

In a multi-unit system, each unit of sale can be related to a common inventory unit by defining a conversion factor. It allows for calculating the quantity of inventory units sold for a particular order in different selling units.

In Solaris, there is a set of selling units for each item, each with a specified conversion factor and price. During the order processing, the selected quantity is converted to the main inventory unit to ensure that the ordered quantity and the converted quantity are consistent. In turn, the converted quantity is used for order processing and inventory management.
Security: Message Authentication and Password Storage

User authentication is an essential aspect of an e-commerce system; thus, passwords should not be stored in plaintext. Instead, a password hashing scheme should be used to store a value that cannot be directly converted into the original password. Current security practices also recommend using dedicated password-hashing algorithms instead of a fast general-purpose hash function. (cheatsheetseries.owasp.org)

Provos and Mazières (1999)[16] proposed bcrypt, which is an adaptive password hashing scheme and provides the cost parameter which can be gradually increased in order to match the rise of computation power and make all password-guessing attempts more expensive. The algorithm also incorporates salt to ensure that the same password with different users will not create the same hash value. (usenix.org)
Solaris uses bcrypt to store user passwords instead of the original value. When a user enters a password, it will be compared to the stored hash value for authentication purposes.
Conversational AI and Tool Calling in Retail

Conversational AI can be applied in various ways within the e-commerce industry. It can be used for search, recommendation, and customer assistance. Rhee and Choi (2020)[8] conducted a study on a conversational voice agent for product recommendations. They analyzed the impact of personalization and social role of the agent on customer’s attitudes toward recommended products.

Liu et al. (2023)[9] created a conversational recommender system based on a large language model (LLM) for e-commerce pre-sales dialogues. They tried to elicit customer requirements and recommendations during conversations and highlighted the limitations of LLMs in terms of domain-specific product recommendation.

LLMs were also found to generate hallucinated information that may differ from the source data. Jiang et al. (2024)[10] investigated the problem of hallucination in product listings enriched with LLMs and tested methods for detecting such data.

Another approach to connecting an LLM with an external database is tool use. Schick et al. (2023)[17] introduced Toolformer and demonstrated how language models could leverage external tools by learning to call APIs and using the obtained responses as inputs for following utterances

In Solaris, the Function Calling (Tool Calling) is utilized to connect the AI assistant with functions in the backend. It allows the assistant to request product, pricing, inventory, and order-related data instead of being limited to text-based interactions. The retrieved information is used within the conversation to fulfill the order.
SYSTEM DESIGN
Overall Architecture

The Solaris platform is implemented as a multi-tier e-commerce system deployed on cloud infrastructure (Figure 3.1). The architecture separates frontend applications, backend business logic, security components, and external services into four main tiers:
Client Presentation Tier: Includes two frontend applications:
Web Shop D2C:   Developed with Next.js 14 using Server-Side Rendering (SSR) for consumer shopping functions.
ERP Admin Portal: Developed with React 18 SPA for warehouse staff, dispatchers, and catalog management.
Gateway & Security Tier: Nginx operates as the entry point for HTTPS requests, managing SSL/TLS termination, CORS configuration, and request forwarding to backend services.
Backend Application Tier (ASP.NET Core .NET 8): Implements business operations based on Clean Architecture principles. The main modules include:
Catalog & Dynamic EAV Module (RQ1): Handles agricultural product attributes and UoM conversion without schema modification.
FEFO Batch & Vault Reservation Module (RQ2): Manages expiry-based inventory selection, stock reservation, and transaction logging.
Single-Hub Logistics Router (RQ3): Calculates delivery distance using the Haversine formula and applies cold-chain delivery constraints.
Conversational AI Sales Assistant (RQ4): Integrates Google Gemini through Tool Calling to retrieve data from SQL Server during conversations.
Persistence & External Cloud Tier:

Microsoft SQL Server stores transactional data, EAV attributes, and inventory transaction records. External integrations include VNPay Sandbox for payment verification and Google Gemini REST API for AI-based customer assistance.

Dynamic Agricultural Attribute Management Using the EAV Model

In traditional relational databases, adding new product attributes usually requires modifying the table schema through ALTER TABLE statements. These changes may acquire Schema Modification locks (Sch-M)[21], which can block database operations and affect system availability. To improve schema flexibility, Solaris adopts a normalized Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) model with three main components:
Entity: Represented by the ProductVariants entity, identifying a specific commercial variant of an agricultural product (e.g., Grade-1 Hoa Loc Mango).
Attribute: Managed within the AttributeDefinitions table, defining catalog-wide technical and biological specifications:

Value: Stored in the ProductVariantAttributeValues table, recording the physical or certified values measured for each variant:
Table 3.2: Concrete EAV Attribute Value Mapping
This architecture enables catalog administrators to introduce new biological specifications via the ERP Admin dashboard instantly, requiring zero structural changes to the production database schema.
Multi-tier Unit of Measure (UoM) and Flexible Packaging Pricing

Agricultural supply chains are frequently characterized by a plethora of measurement units between producers and customers. For instance, cooperatives may be shipping products in bulk (crates, hampers) while customers buy by kilograms or in packages (boxes, pouches).

One approach common in e-commerce is to create different SKUs for different packaging variants. However, this can fragment inventory management, for instance, a warehouse may still have enough inventory in bulk, but a particular package variant is shown as unavailable on an e-commerce website.

FEFO Dispatching and Inventory Concurrency Control
Perishable Expiry Problem and 4-State Inventory Vault Model

The traditional First-In, First-Out (FIFO) method dispatches goods based strictly on chronological receipt dates. However, fresh agricultural produce harvested across different farms often arrives with varying remaining shelf lives due to microclimatic differences and harvesting ripeness. Under FIFO, earlier-received batches with longer shelf lives are dispatched first, leaving newly received but rapidly expiring produce to rot on warehouse shelves, causing substantial shrinkage losses (Ferguson & Ketzenberg, 2006). To eliminate premature spoilage, Solaris enforces the First-Expired, First-Out (FEFO) principle, giving absolute priority to batches with the shortest remaining shelf life.

Concurrency Control and Row-Level Atomic Reservation

During flash sales or when near-expiry inventory becomes limited, multiple customers may attempt checkout simultaneously. Without proper concurrency control, different transactions may read the same available quantity and update inventory at the same time, resulting in negative stock values (overselling anomaly).

Technical Solution: Row-Level Atomic Conditional Update: Solaris handles concurrency control at the database level by using SQL Server row-level exclusive locks (ROWLOCK) within an explicit ACID transaction.

Architectural Impact: Condition evaluation (AND QuantityAvailable >= allocQty) executes atomically with the update operation. The winning transaction updates the row (rowsAffected = 1) and writes to the audit ledger. Any subsequent concurrent transaction targeting the same depleted stock evaluates the predicate as false, resulting in rowsAffected = 0, which immediately triggers an automatic transaction rollback (ROLLBACK) and returns an OutOfStockException (HTTP 400).

Mathematical Safety Invariant:  This mechanism mathematically eliminates negative inventory balances, maintaining a verified 0.00% overselling rate without requiring coarse-grained table locks that degrade throughput.

Accurate distance calculation depends on valid geographic coordinates for the delivery location. Solaris uses a two-tier location resolution approach:

AI Conversational Assistant Design
Tool Calling Architecture and Real-Time Data Grounding

Large language models (LLMs) are based on patterns learned from the training data, and consequently, an LLM can be inaccurate when the training data is not present. In the case of agricultural e-commerce, the LLM can provide incorrect information about the price of products, available stock, and delivery options.

Tool calling (function calling): Instead of using only the knowledge stored in the model, the LLM can make function calls to external services such as a search tool, inventory lookup, and delivery cost calculator.

Data grounding: The Solaris backend is able to run the tools that received the function calls, query the Microsoft SQL Server, and reply with the appropriate information. The information is then used by the LLM to determine the response to the user, which makes it more accurate compared to using only the knowledge stored in the model.

In-Chat Interactive Order Card Component Design

Traditional e-commerce chatbots usually provide product information but require customers to complete purchasing steps through separate pages. This additional navigation increases user effort because customers need to search products again, select packaging units, and provide delivery information manually.

Solaris solves this problem by embedding ordering functionality into the chatbot using Interactive Order Card. The component is implemented as a React component (InteractiveOrderCard) and rendered directly in the chat interface.

Interactive Order Card provides product information, including images, origin certifications, and pricing in Base UoM. Customers can adjust purchase quantities inside the chat interface, while item costs and delivery fees are updated based on the selected quantity and distance calculation.
After confirmation, the request is sent to ConfirmInteractiveOrderAsync , where the backend processes inventory reservation, delivery validation, and payment URL generation.

CONCLUSION
Summary of Research

This study addresses four main technical challenges in agricultural e-commerce: flexible product data and multiple selling units using the EAV model; expiry-aware inventory management using FEFO and inventory reservation; warehouse selection based on product availability and delivery distance; and a database-grounded AI shopping assistant that supports product inquiries and order completion within the chat.
Conclusions

For RQ1, the results show that the combination of EAV and multiple-unit management can support flexible product data in the Solaris system. New product attributes can be added without changing the main product table. Different package sizes can also be converted into a common inventory unit, allowing stock to be managed consistently across different selling units.

For RQ2, the results show that FEFO correctly selects batches with earlier expiration dates before later-expiring batches. The inventory reservation mechanism also maintained consistent stock quantities during the concurrent checkout test with 500 users. No transaction deadlocks, server crashes, or overselling were observed under the tested conditions.

For RQ3, the results show that warehouse selection can consider both product availability and delivery distance. Perishable-product orders outside the predefined 15 km delivery range were rejected, while orders within the range could be assigned to a suitable warehouse. In the multi-item test, the system selected a warehouse with enough stock to fulfill the complete order, avoiding unnecessary order splitting in that scenario.

For RQ4, the results show that integrating the AI assistant with backend functions allowed it to use current product, price, and inventory information during the conversation and support order completion. In the end-to-end checkout test, the AI-assisted flow reduced user interactions by 62.5% and HTTP requests by 57.1% compared with the traditional four-page checkout. The average checkout time was also lower, from 4.48 seconds to 3.63 seconds, and all tested order transactions were completed successfully.
Research Contributions

The primary contribution of this thesis is the design and implementation of a dedicated e-commerce solution for agricultural products, creating a seamless link between the customer-facing storefront and the back-office warehouse management system. Inventory levels, tiered prices, and batch histories remain consistently synchronized throughout the platform. This solution has strong practical value and can be directly adopted by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and agricultural cooperatives seeking to distribute clean food in Vietnam.
Limitations

Despite these results, the project has several limitations due to time and resource constraints. First, the system does not cover the full scope of a standard ERP platform. It currently focuses on warehouse operations, customer management, and basic order accounting. Second, online payments are limited to the VNPAY Sandbox and do not involve real financial transactions.

Internal delivery is also simulated using routing algorithms because the system does not have an actual delivery fleet. Integration with third-party logistics such as Giao Hang Nhanh has limited practical value because perishable products require refrigerated transportation. Finally, the storefront and admin panel are mainly functional and focus on meeting technical requirements rather than providing a fully polished user interface.
Future Work

Several directions can be considered for future development. First, Bluetooth (BLE) or RFID temperature and humidity sensors could be added to motorbike delivery boxes to provide real-time telemetry and improve monitoring of produce conditions beyond the current 15 km radius-based approach. The Google Maps API could also be integrated to allow customers and managers to track delivery locations and routes in real time.

For business operations, the platform could be extended from a procurement-based model to a hybrid model that directly manages partner farms. This would allow product quality to be monitored from cultivation to the final customer within the ERP system. Another direction is to fine-tune a dedicated large language model for Vietnamese agricultural terminology and trading practices. The model could support retail customers on the storefront and assist managers in analyzing internal data.
